units.title: CDC/RDC Architecture and Signoff
units.description: Architect, constrain, verify, and sign off clock- and reset-domain crossings without relying on simulation luck.
units.content:
Clock-domain crossing is a protocol and reliability problem, not merely a two-flop coding pattern. An asynchronous input sampled near a destination edge can violate setup or hold and enter metastability. A synchronizer gives metastability time to resolve; it does not make it impossible. For a single-bit level, a characterized two- or three-stage chain is appropriate when the source level persists long enough to be observed. The first stage must feed only the next stage, with no functional fanout, and implementation constraints must prevent retiming or harmful placement while preserving intended synchronizer recognition. MTBF depends strongly on destination frequency, asynchronous toggle rate, available settling time, and the library's metastability parameters; a chain length is therefore justified by a reliability target, not folklore.

A pulse is not a level. A narrow pulse can be missed entirely, and independently synchronizing related bits can produce incoherent data. Choose a protocol matching the information: toggle or request/acknowledge for sparse events, a handshake for bundled data, or an asynchronous FIFO for sustained traffic. Gray-coded pointers limit adjacent transitions to one bit, but physical skew constraints are still needed so routing does not undermine the one-bit-at-a-time assumption. Prove reset and simultaneous push/pop corner cases, full/empty behavior, and that data remains stable until acknowledgement.

Reset-domain crossings deserve separate analysis. Asynchronous assertion can be necessary, but deassertion should be synchronized independently in each destination domain. Reset release is a timing event: partial release can expose state machines to illegal combinations. Define reset precedence, synchronizer depth, reset values, and whether traffic may start before all participants are ready. RDC tools need intent about asynchronous resets, isolation, and test modes to avoid both false negatives and noisy false positives.

Signoff combines structural CDC/RDC analysis, constraints and waiver review, protocol properties, metastability MTBF assessment, and implementation checks. Review every crossing path by source/destination clocks, data semantics, reset relationship, and receiving protocol. Waivers require an owner, rationale, scope, and proof that the assumed stability or mutual exclusion is real. Re-run after clock, reset, hierarchy, or constraint changes; a clean report is meaningful only when the modeled clocks and exceptions match the delivered design.
keyPoints: Classify the crossing by data semantics and rate before choosing synchronizer structure.
Synchronize reset release independently in each receiving clock domain.
Constrain Gray-pointer skew and protect recognized synchronizer flops from optimization.
Treat waivers and MTBF calculations as documented signoff evidence, not stylistic exceptions.

test.objective: Demonstrate and verify cdc/rdc architecture and signoff behavior against the stated invariants.

questions.question: For an asynchronous status level that remains asserted for many destination cycles, what is the standard first-line structure?
options: A single destination flip-flop with a false-path exception
A destination-clocked two-flop synchronizer chain
A combinational mux controlled by the asynchronous level
Two synchronizers in parallel followed by XOR
questions.explanation: The second stage samples the first after a resolution interval; a false path removes timing analysis but cannot reduce metastability risk.

questions.question: Why must the first synchronizer stage have no functional fanout?
options: Only the next stage should observe its potentially metastable value
It increases the source clock frequency
It guarantees the first stage never becomes metastable
It makes asynchronous reset release synchronous
questions.explanation: A metastable first-stage value must be contained; logic observing it can propagate an uncertain value.

questions.question: A 1 ns pulse arrives asynchronously while the destination period is 10 ns. Which statement is correct?
options: The pulse is guaranteed to be stretched by the first flop
Synchronizer depth guarantees capture independent of pulse width
Adding a false path guarantees capture
A two-flop level synchronizer may miss the pulse completely
questions.explanation: Sampling has no guarantee of observing a pulse shorter than the destination sampling interval; use event transfer protocol or pulse stretching with a proven handshake.

questions.question: A source needs to send a 32-bit word infrequently to another clock domain. Which architecture preserves word coherence?
options: Synchronize only the most significant bit
Combinationally cross the bus and synchronize valid only
Bundled-data handshake holding data stable until acknowledgement
Thirty-two independent two-flop synchronizers
questions.explanation: The handshake synchronizes control while the source holds the bundled bus stable through capture.

questions.question: What property makes Gray-coded FIFO pointers useful across domains?
options: They remove the need to constrain inter-bit routing skew
Adjacent pointer increments change one bit at a time
They eliminate all metastability
They allow binary pointers to be sampled without synchronizers
questions.explanation: A Gray transition changes one bit logically; synchronizers and physical skew constraints are still required.

questions.question: In an asynchronous FIFO, why is a two-flop synchronizer still required on each Gray pointer?
options: A single changing Gray bit can itself be metastable
Gray coding disables all clock-to-Q delay
FIFO pointers are reset asynchronously and therefore need no clocking
It converts the pointer to one-hot encoding
questions.explanation: Gray coding limits ambiguity to adjacent states but does not remove metastability at a sampling edge.

questions.question: What is the primary effect of adding a synchronizer stage?
options: It makes the source and destination clocks frequency-locked
It eliminates the need for CDC structural checks
It guarantees data coherency for arbitrary multi-bit buses
It increases settling time and MTBF at the cost of latency
questions.explanation: Additional settling time reduces failure probability; it does not solve arbitrary bus coherency.

questions.question: Which inputs most strongly affect synchronizer MTBF?
options: Only the source reset value
Only the destination duty cycle, irrespective of frequency
Available resolution time, destination clock rate, and asynchronous toggle rate
RTL line count and signal names
questions.explanation: MTBF models depend on sampling opportunities, transition activity, and exponential resolution time characterized for the cell.

questions.question: Why is asynchronous assertion with synchronous deassertion commonly used for reset?
options: It makes reset values irrelevant
Assertion can act immediately, while synchronized release avoids recovery/removal violations
It prevents the reset pin from reaching the flop
It allows arbitrary clocks to share one deassertion edge
questions.explanation: Immediate assertion is useful for forcing state safe; synchronized release coordinates recovery into each clock domain.

questions.question: Two unrelated destination clocks share one asynchronously deasserted reset. What is the robust release strategy?
options: Use a reset synchronizer per destination domain
Synchronize reset once in the faster domain and fan it out
Remove reset from all data-path state
Gate both clocks until reset toggles twice
questions.explanation: Each domain needs release aligned to its own clock; one domain’s synchronized release is asynchronous to the other.

questions.question: What does a clean CDC tool report fail to prove by itself?
options: That the tool found no structural crossing
That the configured clocks exist
That all unconstrained exceptions are reviewed
That the design meets its functional protocol and reliability requirements
questions.explanation: Structural recognition does not prove pulse capture, data stability, reset sequencing, or a target MTBF.

questions.question: Why should a CDC waiver include scope and rationale?
options: To avoid writing assertions
To make the crossing synchronous by declaration
To make assumptions reviewable and prevent a broad waiver hiding unrelated crossings
To suppress all future reports regardless of hierarchy
questions.explanation: A narrowly scoped waiver identifies the exact justified crossing and preserves visibility of new or changed paths.

questions.question: What is unsafe about independently synchronizing every bit of a changing binary counter?
options: The receiving clock cannot sample vectors
Different bits can settle on different cycles and form a value never sent
Binary counters cannot toggle more than one bit
Synchronizers force all bits to share clock skew
questions.explanation: Each bit is metastability-contained independently, but there is no atomic snapshot or coherency guarantee.

questions.question: A toggle synchronizer transfers an event. What source-side condition is needed?
options: The toggle must not change again before destination logic detects the prior change
The toggle must pulse high for one source cycle only
The clocks must have equal periods
The destination must use combinational edge detection
questions.explanation: If toggles occur twice before sampling, the destination can observe no net change; throughput needs acknowledgement or rate bounds.

questions.question: If a handshake acknowledgement can arrive while a new request is launched, what should be checked?
options: The data bus is randomized every cycle regardless of valid
The request and acknowledgement use identical clock pins
The synchronizer stages are assigned blocking assignments
No event is lost or duplicated under simultaneous state transitions
questions.explanation: Simultaneous transitions often expose protocol bugs; prove accepted-event accounting and stable bundled data.

questions.question: Which implementation treatment is appropriate for recognized synchronizer registers?
options: Add arbitrary false paths between synchronizer stages
Mark every source register as asynchronous logic
Preserve intended chain placement/recognition and prohibit retiming across stages
Allow retiming to merge the stages into one register
questions.explanation: The chain depends on sequential settling time; synthesis/physical optimization must not collapse or reorder it.

questions.question: What does a false-path constraint on an asynchronous input accomplish?
options: Proves the receiving logic is stable
Excludes meaningless phase-based setup analysis on the async path, not metastability prevention
Prevents input transitions during the capture aperture
Enforces a minimum pulse width
questions.explanation: False paths are analysis controls; the synchronizer architecture and reliability analysis address metastability.

questions.question: A reset release causes a one-cycle illegal FSM state only in silicon. Which investigation is most relevant?
options: Check reset recovery/removal, per-domain deassertion, and reset-domain interactions
Increase simulation random seed count only
Relax all clock uncertainty
Replace nonblocking assignments with blocking assignments
questions.explanation: Asynchronous release can violate recovery/removal and different state elements may leave reset inconsistently.

questions.question: What is essential when waiving a multi-bit CDC because data is “stable”?
options: Assume stable because the bus name contains _hold
Synchronize only the parity bit
Set the path false in every mode without review
Prove and assert the stability window spans destination capture
questions.explanation: The bundled-data assumption must be guaranteed by a source protocol and checked under the actual operating conditions.

questions.question: Which change should trigger CDC/RDC signoff rerun?
options: Renaming a local variable with no elaboration effect
Changing waveform colors in a viewer
Changing clock/reset topology, hierarchy, or relevant constraints
Changing a comment in an unrelated test
questions.explanation: Analysis depends on clocks, resets, structure, and constraints; design or intent changes can invalidate prior evidence.

units.title: High-Throughput Pipelines and Backpressure
units.description: Design elastic pipelines that sustain throughput while preserving ordering, data integrity, and bounded-resource behavior.
units.content:
High-throughput design is about the rate at which work is accepted and retired, not simply the number of pipeline registers. A latency-L pipeline can accept one item per cycle when every stage can advance independently and downstream capacity is available. Backpressure couples that capacity information upstream. A stage holding valid data must keep its payload and sideband metadata stable while blocked; otherwise a downstream consumer can see a changing transaction despite valid remaining asserted. Treat each stage as an elastic buffer with an explicit occupancy invariant.

For a one-entry stage, transfer occurs on valid && ready. On a clock edge, a new item may replace the old one when the old item transfers; requiring an empty cycle between items needlessly limits throughput to one item every two cycles. Conversely, blindly asserting ready when full can overwrite a stalled item. A skid buffer captures a transaction that has already crossed a combinational ready boundary when downstream stalls, breaking a long combinational path without losing data. Buffer depth must be derived from in-flight work and latency, not guessed.

Combinational ready chains can create timing loops, long paths, or poor physical locality. Registering ready adds a cycle of feedback latency and therefore requires enough buffering to absorb the extra in-flight transactions. Throughput, latency, initiation interval, and buffer capacity are different metrics. For example, a three-cycle pipeline with initiation interval one has three-cycle minimum latency but can retire one item each cycle after fill. A globally stalled pipeline may preserve correctness yet fail performance goals; quantify stall duty, average occupancy, and required bandwidth.

Verification should account for every accepted item exactly once, in order, including simultaneous dequeue/enqueue, reset, full, empty, and prolonged stalls. Scoreboards compare payload and metadata at handshakes, not at arbitrary cycles. Assertions check stable output while blocked and ensure occupancy remains bounded. For multiple producers or variable-latency units, include arbitration fairness and response matching. Physical signoff must examine the ready path, buffering, fanout, and clock load as carefully as forward data latency.
keyPoints: Define acceptance and retirement only at valid/ready handshakes.
A blocked valid transaction holds payload and metadata stable until accepted.
Size elastic/skid storage to cover registered backpressure latency and in-flight work.
Measure initiation interval, latency, occupancy, and stall behavior separately.

test.objective: Demonstrate and verify high-throughput pipelines and backpressure behavior against the stated invariants.

questions.question: A four-stage pipeline accepts one token each cycle after startup. What is its initiation interval and minimum latency?
options: II=1 cycle; latency=1 cycle
II=4 cycles; latency=4 cycles
II=1 cycle; latency=4 cycles
II=4 cycles; latency=1 cycle
questions.explanation: Independent stage advance permits one new token per cycle; the four registered stages still impose four-cycle latency under this convention.

questions.question: For a one-entry elastic stage, why is ready often defined as !full || out_ready?
options: It makes out_valid combinationally depend on input data
It allows a departing item to be replaced on the same edge
It permits overwrite even if the downstream is stalled
It prevents simultaneous enqueue and dequeue
questions.explanation: When full and downstream ready, the stored token retires at that edge, so a new token can fill the freed slot without a bubble.

questions.question: While out_valid=1 and out_ready=0, what is the key source-side invariant?
options: Payload and associated metadata remain stable
Payload changes each cycle to test the receiver
out_valid must deassert after one cycle
The producer may count the item as retired
questions.explanation: The transaction has not transferred until the handshake; changing it violates the consumer’s stalled-item contract.

questions.question: A ready signal is registered, adding one cycle to backpressure propagation. What architectural consequence follows?
options: Throughput necessarily doubles
No extra capacity is ever required
All valid signals should become combinational
More in-flight items may arrive, so buffering must absorb them
questions.explanation: Upstream may continue sending before it observes the registered stop; storage must cover this feedback latency.

questions.question: What problem does a skid buffer principally solve?
options: Eliminates the need for valid
Guarantees zero-cycle latency across a clock domain
Captures an in-flight item when registered/late backpressure arrives
Reorders responses to reduce latency
questions.explanation: It absorbs a transaction that crossed the ready boundary before the stall propagated, while helping break long ready paths.

questions.question: For a stream with a 25% average stall fraction, what is the ideal long-run service rate if one item is consumed per unstalled cycle?
options: 0.25 cycles per item
0.75 items per cycle
4 items per cycle
1.25 items per cycle
questions.explanation: Under the stated independent-rate assumption, only 75% of cycles service an item; burst correlations may affect finite-window results.

questions.question: What does “latency 3, initiation interval 1” mean?
options: Each item takes three cycles, but a new item can start every cycle
Each item takes one cycle and a new item every three cycles
Three items are accepted only after three idle cycles
The pipeline must have exactly three buffer entries
questions.explanation: Latency is per-token delay; initiation interval is spacing between accepted tokens.

questions.question: When should a scoreboard remove an expected token from its queue?
options: As soon as output valid rises, even if stalled
When input valid is asserted regardless of ready
After a fixed latency, regardless of stalls
On the observed output valid && ready handshake
questions.explanation: Backpressure makes fixed-cycle matching incorrect; retirement occurs only on handshake.

questions.question: Which corner case is most likely to reveal a one-entry buffer bubble or overwrite?
options: Input invalid and output not ready forever
Only isolated transfers into an empty stage
Full stage simultaneously drains and accepts a replacement
Reset held permanently low
questions.explanation: Simultaneous dequeue/enqueue tests replacement logic and exposes incorrect ready/full updates.

questions.question: A two-entry FIFO has occupancy 2 and receives push=1,pop=1. What is next occupancy?
questions.explanation: The accepted push and pop cancel; the FIFO remains full after both legal transfers.

questions.question: Why is asserting ready unconditionally on a full buffer unsafe?
options: A stalled current item can be overwritten before it is consumed
It creates excessive output latency
It blocks all new producers permanently
It converts synchronous logic to asynchronous logic
questions.explanation: Ready is a promise of capacity; unconditional assertion when no replaceable slot exists violates that promise.

questions.question: A design is correct under stall but falls to one transfer every two cycles with no stalls. Which metric is deficient?
options: Transaction ordering
Reset assertion time
Payload width
Initiation interval / peak throughput
questions.explanation: The avoidable empty-cycle bubble raises initiation interval to two even though steady-state capacity should be one per cycle.

questions.question: For a 3-cycle registered stop path and upstream rate of one item/cycle, how many additional slots may be needed?
options: One bit per payload bit
Three stages of synchronizers
Up to three items already in flight, depending on where the stop is observed
Exactly zero, because ready is registered
questions.explanation: The upstream can send during the propagation delay; count actual transfer opportunities along the feedback path and provide matching capacity.

questions.question: What is the strongest useful assertion for a stalled output?
options: $stable(payload) |-> valid==0
valid && !ready |=> valid && $stable(payload)
valid |-> !ready
ready |=> !valid
questions.explanation: The next sampled cycle must still present the same unconsumed transaction; reset/disable conditions should be specified for the environment.

questions.question: A scoreboard reports duplicate output payload values. Why must it track transaction identity or full expected sequence?
options: Equal payloads can be legal distinct transactions; value-only duplicate detection is ambiguous
Payloads are always unique in a valid protocol
Handshake signals cannot be monitored
It is impossible to compare streams under stalls
questions.explanation: Repeated data values may be valid, so compare ordered expected items or attach unique IDs rather than infer duplication from equality.

questions.question: How does long combinational ready chaining hurt implementation?
options: It removes all clock-to-Q delay
It guarantees constant latency independent of stalls
It prevents any combinational loops
It can create long critical paths and placement/fanout pressure
questions.explanation: The backward capacity path can become a timing bottleneck and physically span many stages.

questions.question: What should a bounded-occupancy assertion use as its update events?
options: Clock transitions on both interfaces
Payload changes
Accepted push and pop handshakes
Raw valid assertions, regardless of ready
questions.explanation: Occupancy changes only when transfers are accepted, so raw intent signals overcount blocked attempts.

questions.question: What is required if two pipelines merge into one output?
options: Drop ready from one source
Arbitration plus fair or bounded-starvation policy and per-source accounting
OR the valid signals and concatenate payloads
Synchronize every data bit independently
questions.explanation: A shared resource needs a defined selection policy and tests that no source is starved or duplicated.

questions.question: Why is a fixed-delay testbench comparison fragile for an elastic pipeline?
options: Backpressure changes retirement cycle while preserving order
An elastic pipeline has no clock
Payload widths vary each cycle
Ready cannot be randomized
questions.explanation: Variable stalls alter latency; handshake-driven queue comparison checks functional equivalence independent of timing.

questions.question: What does a throughput result of one item/cycle say about latency?
options: It proves latency equals one cycle
It proves there is no buffering
It proves the path is combinational
Nothing by itself; high throughput can coexist with many cycles of latency
questions.explanation: Throughput is steady-state rate while latency is per-item delay; they are independent design dimensions.

units.title: Ready/Valid and AXI-Lite-Class Protocols
units.description: Apply synchronous ready/valid transfer semantics and AXI-Lite-class channel rules to robust register interfaces.
units.content:
Ready/valid is a local synchronous transfer contract. A beat transfers on a rising edge where valid and ready are both high. The source owns valid and payload: once it presents a beat, it holds valid and all payload fields stable until the handshake. The sink owns ready and may vary it according to capacity. A source must not wait for ready before asserting valid if that creates a deadlock with a sink that waits for valid before asserting ready. Registered interfaces can add latency, but must preserve these ownership rules.

AXI-Lite uses five independent channels: write address (AW), write data (W), write response (B), read address (AR), and read data/response (R). AW and W are independent; a manager can present them in either order or concurrently, and the subordinate must capture each only on its own handshake. A common bug assumes simultaneous AWVALID and WVALID. Another is issuing BVALID before both halves of a write have been accepted. The subordinate must hold BVALID and BRESP stable until BREADY. Similarly, RVALID, RDATA, and RRESP remain stable under R backpressure.

One outstanding write response or read response may be sufficient for a small control block, but that is an explicit capacity limit. Correctness includes ordering, response generation, and preventing acceptance of more work than can be tracked. Byte strobes select which bytes change; unstrobed register bits must retain their prior value. Address decode should use aligned word addresses and report invalid accesses consistently. Reset values and side effects such as clear-on-read require a defined timing point: typically the AR handshake, not when ARVALID first appears.

Verification should vary AW/W ordering, independent channel stalls, simultaneous read and write, partial strobes, invalid addresses, reset, and held VALID. Scoreboards should model register state and expected responses, while assertions cover stability and eventual response under fairness assumptions. A protocol checker cannot establish the software-visible meaning of a register map; that requires a specified contract. Avoid combinational paths between interface inputs and outputs when prohibited by the integration profile, and document whether throughput allows a new transaction in the same cycle an old one retires.
keyPoints: A transfer occurs only at a sampling edge with both VALID and READY high.
The source holds VALID and all payload fields stable while waiting.
AXI-Lite AW and W are independent and must be buffered/paired independently.
Honor byte strobes, response backpressure, address validity, and specified side-effect timing.

test.objective: Demonstrate and verify ready/valid and axi-lite-class protocols behavior against the stated invariants.

questions.question: At which event does a ready/valid beat transfer?
options: When valid first rises, irrespective of ready
When ready rises, irrespective of valid
At the falling edge after valid remains high
A rising edge with valid and ready both asserted
questions.explanation: The handshake is sampled synchronously on the active clock edge when both control signals are high.

questions.question: A source has a beat but READY is low for five cycles. What must it do?
options: Change payload each stalled cycle
Count the transfer on the first VALID cycle
Keep VALID and payload stable until a handshake
Withdraw VALID after one cycle
questions.explanation: The sink has not accepted the beat; source-side contract requires the same transaction remain offered.

questions.question: Why is waiting for READY before asserting VALID potentially deadlocking?
options: The protocol requires both signals to be low at reset
A sink may wait for VALID before asserting READY
READY is always asynchronous
VALID must be delayed exactly one cycle
questions.explanation: If each side waits for the other to act first, neither starts; the source should present valid independently of ready.

questions.question: In AXI-Lite, what does independence of AW and W mean?
options: Address and data may handshake in different cycles and either order
They must always be asserted simultaneously
They share a single READY signal by definition
The write response precedes both requests
questions.explanation: Each channel has its own VALID/READY handshake; pairing requires tracking accepted address and data.

questions.question: When may a subordinate safely assert BVALID for a write?
options: As soon as AWVALID is observed without handshake
Before WVALID if BREADY is high
Only in the same cycle as AWREADY
After both AW and W transfers for that transaction have been accepted
questions.explanation: A write response acknowledges the complete write request, which requires accepted address and data.

questions.question: BVALID is high and BREADY is low. Which behavior is required?
options: Change BRESP to the next transaction
Accept another write and overwrite the response
Hold BVALID and BRESP stable until the response handshake
Withdraw BVALID and retry later
questions.explanation: A valid response is an offered transaction and must remain unchanged under backpressure.

questions.question: When should a clear-on-read side effect usually take effect?
options: At any combinational address transition
At the defined accepted read event, commonly AR handshake or response contract point
Whenever ARVALID is high, even if ARREADY is low
Only when RREADY is low
questions.explanation: The specification must identify the event; applying on an unaccepted request can cause repeated side effects during stalls.

questions.question: A byte-strobe write has WSTRB=0101. What should happen to unstrobed bytes?
options: Retain their previous values
Be cleared to zero
Take values from adjacent address
Become unknown by protocol
questions.explanation: WSTRB qualifies byte lanes; only enabled bytes are updated.

questions.question: A design captures AW only when AWVALID && WVALID. What valid traffic does it mishandle?
options: AW and W always handshake together
No read can ever complete
BREADY asserted early
AW may handshake before WVALID arrives
questions.explanation: AW and W are independent; the address may legally be accepted before data is offered.

questions.question: A register block accepts one read but has a pending RVALID under stall. What is safe capacity behavior?
options: Drop RVALID until RREADY
Force RREADY high internally
Do not accept another read unless it can track it without overwriting the pending response
Overwrite RDATA with the new address result
questions.explanation: The subordinate must preserve response information; acceptance should be limited to available tracking/storage resources.

questions.question: Why should address decode account for alignment?
options: It avoids synchronizer metastability
Unaligned addresses may select an unintended register or violate the interface contract
Alignment changes the handshake definition
AXI-Lite only permits byte addresses to be 0
questions.explanation: Register word decode should map legal aligned offsets explicitly and define behavior for unsupported addresses.

questions.question: A manager holds ARVALID but ARREADY stays low. What response signal may the subordinate assert for that unaccepted request?
options: No response is required until the request handshake
RVALID must assert immediately
RDATA must change with ARADDR
BVALID must assert as a substitute
questions.explanation: The request has not transferred; response generation before accepted request risks duplicates or stale data.

questions.question: What is the correct monitor accounting point for a write address?
options: AWVALID high at any time
WVALID && WREADY
BVALID && BREADY
AWVALID && AWREADY at the active edge
questions.explanation: Only the AW channel handshake constitutes acceptance of the address.

questions.question: What is a useful AXI-Lite write stress case?
options: Only reset cycles
Read transactions with all READY signals tied high
AW first, W delayed, then independent B backpressure
AW and W always together with BREADY always high
questions.explanation: Independent delays expose implementations that accidentally assume coupled request channels or unstallable responses.

questions.question: An invalid register address is accessed. What must be determined from the specification?
options: It becomes a CDC crossing
Defined error response and side-effect behavior
The subordinate must hang forever
The manager may infer zero response
questions.explanation: Illegal-access behavior is part of the programming contract; a deterministic error response is typical.

questions.question: In same-cycle response retirement and new request acceptance, what must be ensured?
options: Old response data is not overwritten before its handshake and tracking capacity is updated atomically
New request always has priority, regardless of old response
VALID can be deasserted combinationally after sampling
Both transactions get identical IDs
questions.explanation: Simultaneous events need deliberate next-state logic to preserve the retiring response and correctly allocate capacity.

questions.question: Which property captures a held read response?
options: ARVALID |-> !RREADY
RREADY |=> !RVALID
RDATA==$past(RDATA) always
RVALID && !RREADY |=> RVALID && $stable({RDATA,RRESP})
questions.explanation: Under response backpressure the offer persists with stable data/response; disable or reset behavior should be modeled.

questions.question: What does a bus protocol checker not prove?
options: That payload holds while stalled
That response channels obey ready/valid
That each register’s software-visible semantics match the product specification
That channel handshake timing follows assertions
questions.explanation: Protocol legality and functional register-map correctness are distinct verification obligations.

questions.question: A two-bit strobe updates only byte 0, but RTL also modifies a write-one-to-clear status bit. What is the issue?
options: READY must be low during writes
Side-effect semantics and strobes must be specified per register bit/field
WSTRB has no meaning in AXI-Lite
Status bits cannot be written
questions.explanation: Register-specific semantics can qualify effects differently; a generic write mask may accidentally clear or set status fields.

questions.question: What is needed to prove an eventual response property under arbitrary stalls?
options: An environment fairness assumption that READY eventually becomes high
A two-state simulator
Tie READY low permanently
Ignore response VALID
questions.explanation: No implementation can force progress if the manager refuses to accept a response forever; liveness proof needs fair readiness.

units.title: Temporal SVA and Formal Verification
units.description: Turn interface and state-machine contracts into sound temporal properties, assumptions, and bounded or unbounded proofs.
units.content:
Temporal verification is strongest when each property is tied to an explicit clock, reset policy, and environmental contract. In SystemVerilog Assertions, a sampled expression is evaluated at a clocking event; concurrent assertions use sampled values rather than ordinary procedural observation. `|->` starts the consequent in the same sampled cycle as the antecedent match, whereas `|=>` starts on the next sampled cycle. A property such as `valid && !ready |=> valid && $stable(data)` states that a stalled offer persists into the next sample. It should be disabled or conditioned across reset according to the design’s reset contract.

Sequences describe temporal patterns; repetition operators have distinct meanings. `[*N]` is consecutive repetition, `[->N]` is a goto repetition with the final match at the last occurrence, and `[=N]` permits trailing nonmatches in a sequence context. `$past` refers to a previous sampled value and is undefined or tool-dependent before sufficient history exists unless guarded with a past-valid flag. `$rose`, `$fell`, and `$stable` also operate on sampled values. Be careful with vacuity: implication passes whenever its antecedent never occurs. Cover properties, antecedent coverage, and nonvacuous checks ensure the scenario was reachable.

Formal tools explore all allowed input sequences, so unconstrained inputs often create physically impossible behavior or state-space explosion. Assumptions should encode only true environment obligations—for example, stable payload while valid is stalled or legal reset sequencing. Assuming the DUT’s desired response can make a broken implementation “prove.” Assertions describe guarantees; assumptions describe environment restrictions; covers request witness traces. Safety properties say something bad never happens and often have finite counterexamples. Liveness properties require eventual progress, usually under fairness assumptions; a permanently deasserted READY makes response completion impossible to guarantee.

Bounded model checking proves properties only within a bound unless completeness is established. Induction requires an invariant strong enough to connect arbitrary reachable states to successors. Counterexample triage checks reset initialization, assumptions, abstraction, and the first diverging cycle before changing RTL. Proof signoff records tool/version, elaboration defines, clocks, reset model, assumptions, exclusions, property coverage, and unresolved failures. Assertions are executable design contracts, not decorative comments; review them as carefully as the RTL.
keyPoints: State the sampling clock, reset disable semantics, and antecedent activation explicitly.
Distinguish overlapped implication from non-overlapped implication and sampled-time delays.
Check vacuity and cover reachable antecedent/consequent scenarios.
Separate DUT guarantees, environment assumptions, and progress fairness constraints.

test.objective: Demonstrate and verify temporal sva and formal verification behavior against the stated invariants.
test.integrationAssumptions: Icarus Verilog does not support the concurrent SVA used by sva_contract; its procedural tb_sva_contract alone is not an assertion check. Run the example and testbench with an IEEE 1800 concurrent-assertion simulator such as Questa, VCS, or Xcelium, enabling assertions (for Questa: vlog -sv sva_contract.sv tb_sva_contract.sv; vsim -c -assert work.tb_sva_contract -do "run -all; quit -f"). For formal verification, load sva_contract with a formal harness in a property-capable tool such as JasperGold or VC Formal, define the destination clock and reset/initial-state model, prove a_hold_while_stalled, and cover c_stall_seen; do not treat the delay-based simulation testbench as synthesizable formal stimulus. Assume reset is eventually released and that the interface is sampled on each rising edge; the assertion is a DUT guarantee, not an environmental assumption.

questions.question: In a concurrent property, when does `A |=> B` sample B relative to a matched A?
options: On the next clocking event
On the same clocking event
Only when A falls
At an arbitrary delta cycle
questions.explanation: Non-overlapped implication starts the consequent one sampled cycle after the antecedent match.

questions.question: What does `A |-> B` mean for a single-cycle antecedent?
options: B begins one sampled cycle later
B is required before A
B is required only if A never occurs
B is required in the same sampled cycle as A
questions.explanation: Overlapped implication aligns the consequent start with the antecedent match.

questions.question: Why can an implication assertion pass vacuously?
options: It has too many clock edges
The assertion always forces the antecedent true
Its antecedent may never match
The simulator ignores all consequents
questions.explanation: Implication is satisfied when its antecedent is false; coverage should confirm the intended trigger occurred.

questions.question: What does `disable iff (!rst_n)` do to an assertion?
options: Makes all inputs unconstrained forever
Aborts/disables attempts while reset condition is true
Samples the property on reset falling edge only
Asserts reset is eventually deasserted
questions.explanation: The disable condition suppresses active property evaluation during the specified reset interval.

questions.question: What is the role of a `cover property` next to an assertion?
options: Show that an interesting temporal scenario is reachable/observed
Constrain the DUT to behave correctly
Turn a failed assertion into a pass
Prove all states are reachable
questions.explanation: Covers provide witness reachability information and help expose vacuous proofs.

questions.question: A property uses `$past(x)` on the first active cycle. What is a concern?
options: $past always means the current value
It introduces asynchronous sampling
It changes x in the DUT
There may be no valid previous sampled value; guard history
questions.explanation: Past-value functions need valid sampled history; a past-valid flag avoids startup ambiguity.

questions.question: Which operator expresses N consecutive matches?
questions.explanation: Consecutive repetition requires each successive sampled element to match.

questions.question: Which sequence repetition permits intervening nonmatches before the final required occurrence?
options: First_match only
Throughout
questions.explanation: Goto repetition counts occurrences with the final match at the last occurrence; consecutive repetition would reject gaps.

questions.question: What does an assumption mean in formal verification?
options: A restriction on legal environment behavior
A guarantee made by the DUT
A cover request for a trace
A reset value for state
questions.explanation: Assumptions constrain inputs/initial conditions and must be justified by the system contract.

questions.question: What is a dangerous consequence of assuming `valid |-> ready` for the DUT interface?
options: It increases solver coverage automatically
It proves ready is always low
It models reset recovery
It can exclude legal stalls and hide a stability bug
questions.explanation: If the environment is allowed to stall, the assumption rules out precisely the cases needed to verify backpressure behavior.

questions.question: Why is a safety property often amenable to bounded counterexample search?
options: It can only be proven by simulation
It has no state-space representation
A finite bad prefix demonstrates the violation
It always requires fairness
questions.explanation: A safety violation has a finite trace showing the first bad state or event.

questions.question: What does liveness usually require to prove eventual response?
options: No assumptions of any kind
Fairness assumptions that the environment eventually permits progress
A permanently blocked receiver
Only a combinational assertion
questions.explanation: Progress cannot be guaranteed if the environment can block the necessary handshake forever.

questions.question: What does bounded model checking through depth 20 establish by itself?
options: No counterexample within the explored bound, not necessarily an unbounded proof
An inductive proof for every future cycle
That all state bits are initialized
That the simulation testbench is correct
questions.explanation: A finite bound does not imply completeness unless a completeness threshold or induction proof is established.

questions.question: Why might induction fail even when a design is correct?
options: The clock is too slow
The testbench has too many transactions
An assertion is syntactically valid
The candidate invariant is too weak to relate arbitrary states to reachable successors
questions.explanation: Induction considers states beyond the reachable set; strengthening invariants may be needed to exclude spurious transitions.

questions.question: A property checks `valid && !ready |=> valid && $stable(data)`. What common gap remains?
options: It constrains source behavior
It checks data parity
No check that the antecedent ever occurs
It proves transfer ordering across all channels
questions.explanation: Implication can pass vacuously if the design never stalls; add a cover or targeted stimulus.

questions.question: How should reset be treated in a proof?
options: Ignore reset because formal is not simulation
Model reset initialization and deassertion according to actual design/environment behavior
Assume every state bit is zero without modeling reset
Disable all assertions permanently
questions.explanation: Reset semantics determine reachable states and release behavior; unrealistic initialization can hide or invent bugs.

questions.question: A counterexample diverges only before reset is released. What should be checked first?
options: Whether reset assumptions and initialization match the intended system contract
Whether assertion naming follows style
Whether output waveform uses binary
Whether all inputs are tied high
questions.explanation: Formal traces may exploit unconstrained startup; validate reset modeling before diagnosing an RTL defect.

questions.question: Which property is a guarantee rather than an assumption for a compliant source?
options: READY eventually rises, absent a system fairness obligation
Reset is never asserted
Input data is never X in silicon
VALID and payload remain stable while VALID&&!READY
questions.explanation: A source guarantee describes DUT behavior; READY progress is an environmental condition unless the design controls it.

questions.question: Why record elaboration defines and tool version in proof signoff?
options: They replace assertion coverage
They ensure no counterexamples are possible
They affect the elaborated design and proof interpretation/reproducibility
They alter the formal clock frequency
questions.explanation: A proof applies to the specific configuration and tool semantics used; reproducibility requires preserving that context.

questions.question: What is the first useful step for a failing property counterexample?
options: Increase proof depth without reading the trace
Find the earliest divergence and inspect assumptions, reset, and sampled timing
Immediately weaken the assertion
Delete the failing cover
questions.explanation: The shortest causal prefix often distinguishes an actual design bug from a modeling or sampling mistake.

units.title: Scalable UVM Verification Architecture
units.description: Build maintainable UVM environments that scale across configurations, transaction complexity, reuse, and coverage closure.
units.content:
A scalable UVM environment separates stimulus intent from pin-level mechanics. A sequence creates transaction objects; a sequencer arbitrates them; a driver converts items into timed interface activity; a monitor reconstructs observed transactions from handshakes. Monitors should be passive and reusable, and scoreboards should consume observed—not merely requested—transactions. This separation lets the same agent operate as active or passive and prevents the test’s expected behavior from being coupled to a buggy driver.

Agents contain a configuration object describing virtual interfaces, active/passive mode, protocol features, and address or timing parameters. Configuration must be established before component build/connect phases, and virtual interfaces should be checked for null rather than silently substituted. The environment’s build phase constructs topology; connect phase wires analysis ports and exports; run phase launches concurrent behavior; check/report phases summarize results. Factory overrides enable targeted specialization, but excessive global overrides obscure which implementation is active. Prefer component-local configuration and explicit type overrides with auditability.

Analysis ports broadcast immutable observed transactions to independent consumers such as a scoreboard, coverage collector, and protocol checker. A scoreboard predicts from a reference model and compares accepted/retired behavior; it must account for latency, reordering, reset, and simultaneous events. If transactions can be outstanding, match by ID or protocol order rather than a single “last expected” variable. Concurrency uses objections to keep the phase alive while required work completes; raised objections need bounded, justified drop paths. A test that hangs waiting on an unbounded sequence is a verification infrastructure failure, not a passing test.

Random stimulus is useful only when constrained by legal protocol rules and measured by coverage. Seed reproducibility requires recording the simulator, seed, test, plusargs, configuration, and source revision. Functional coverage models scenarios and crosses that matter; code coverage alone does not establish requirement coverage. Coverage closure examines unreachable bins, missing stimulus, and specification relevance rather than waiving bins indiscriminately. Regression architecture should isolate tests, bound runtime, classify failures, and avoid global state that makes results order-dependent. Reusable agents need documented assumptions, analysis semantics, and reset behavior so integration environments do not infer an unintended contract.
keyPoints: Keep sequence intent, driver pin timing, monitor observation, and scoreboard prediction separate.
Use checked configuration objects and explicit virtual-interface propagation before run phase.
Scoreboard from observed handshakes and support outstanding IDs, reset, and legal reordering.
Treat functional coverage, reproducible seeds, bounded objections, and failure classification as signoff artifacts.

test.objective: Demonstrate and verify scalable uvm verification architecture behavior against the stated invariants.
test.integrationAssumptions: Icarus Verilog can run the plain procedural tb_uvm_contract smoke test but does not provide the UVM class library/runtime needed for rv_item and rv_monitor. Run that standalone exercise with iverilog -g2012 -s tb_uvm_contract -o tb_uvm_contract.vvp exercise.sv && vvp tb_uvm_contract.vvp. To exercise the UVM architecture example, use an IEEE 1800.2-capable UVM simulator/environment such as Questa with its bundled UVM library, VCS/UVM, or Xcelium/UVM. Compile rv_if before the UVM classes and include the simulator-supported uvm_pkg/UVM library; add a top-level UVM test that instantiates rv_if and the DUT, places the interface in uvm_config_db before run_phase, creates the monitor, connects its analysis port to a scoreboard/subscriber, and runs a sequence with VALID/payload held stable until VALID && READY at a rising edge. Execute that test through the simulator UVM runner (for Questa, compile with vlog -sv and the bundled UVM package, then run vsim -c -uvm <top> -do "run -all; quit -f"); the test should report the scoreboard PASS and terminate with bounded objections. The module tb_uvm_contract is a separate handshake scoreboard smoke test, not itself a UVM test.

questions.question: Which component should convert a sequence item into pin-level timing?
options: Scoreboard
Driver
Monitor
Coverage subscriber
questions.explanation: The driver owns active pin-level behavior; monitors observe it without driving DUT signals.

questions.question: What should a passive monitor publish?
options: Transactions reconstructed from actual interface handshakes
The sequence items before they reach the DUT
Predicted register values only
Random values unrelated to observed signals
questions.explanation: Observed handshakes provide independent evidence of what the DUT interface actually accepted or produced.

questions.question: Why should a scoreboard consume monitor output rather than sequence requests?
options: Sequences cannot be randomized
Monitors are always active drivers
Analysis ports modify DUT outputs
The driver or DUT may fail, so requests do not prove acceptance
questions.explanation: Observed transactions allow comparison against actual accepted/retired behavior, exposing lost or malformed requests.

questions.question: In which phase is component topology normally created?
options: report_phase
final_phase only
build_phase
run_phase
questions.explanation: Build phase constructs components; run phase executes concurrent stimulus and monitoring.

questions.question: What is the purpose of connect_phase?
options: Generate coverage bins automatically
Wire ports, exports, and TLM connections after construction
Start random sequences
Destroy components
questions.explanation: Connect phase joins already-created components and their communication paths.

questions.question: When should a virtual interface be validated?
options: During configuration/build before run-time use
After the test completes
Only when the first fatal occurs
Never; UVM supplies it automatically
questions.explanation: Early checking produces a clear configuration failure rather than a null access during simulation.

questions.question: Why configure an agent active or passive?
options: Disable all analysis transactions
Make a scoreboard random
Change clock frequency globally
Reuse the same monitor/protocol model without driving pins in passive contexts
questions.explanation: An agent can monitor a connected DUT passively or drive an interface actively depending on environment role.

questions.question: What is the best use of an analysis port?
options: Drive backpressure directly
Store a global singleton scoreboard
Broadcast observed transactions to independent subscribers
Arbitrate sequence requests
questions.explanation: Analysis ports support decoupled one-to-many transaction observation.

questions.question: A protocol permits responses out of order with IDs. How should the scoreboard match them?
options: By sorting response payload numerically
By transaction ID and expected response model
By assuming FIFO order unconditionally
By comparing only the most recent item
questions.explanation: IDs identify outstanding requests and enable correct association when completion order differs.

questions.question: What common error can produce a permanently hung UVM test?
options: An objection is raised without a bounded drop path
An analysis port has two subscribers
A sequence item is factory-created
A coverage collector samples a handshake
questions.explanation: An unbalanced or unbounded objection prevents the phase from ending.

questions.question: What should a functional coverage cross represent?
options: Every signal combination regardless of relevance
Source-code line coverage only
A substitute for a scoreboard
A meaningful combination of requirement scenarios
questions.explanation: Cross coverage records combinations that matter to specified behaviors, not merely arbitrary Cartesian products.

questions.question: Why is code coverage not equivalent to requirements coverage?
options: Requirements cannot be tested
Every code line maps one-to-one to a requirement
Executed statements may not demonstrate required scenarios or corner-case outcomes
Code coverage counts only assertions
questions.explanation: Coverage of implementation structure does not ensure all specified behavior was exercised and checked.

questions.question: Which metadata is needed to reproduce a randomized failure?
options: A count of passed tests
Seed, simulator/configuration, test, plusargs, and source revision
Only the waveform filename
Only the UVM agent name
questions.explanation: Randomization and elaboration depend on more than seed alone; capture execution context to replay reliably.

questions.question: Why can broad global factory overrides hurt reuse?
options: They obscure which component implementation is instantiated and where behavior changes
They prevent any component reuse
They disable transaction randomization
They guarantee faster simulation
questions.explanation: Unscoped overrides can silently affect multiple environments and make topology harder to reason about.

questions.question: What is a good response to an uncovered functional bin?
options: Delete every uncovered bin
Assume code coverage proves it
Mark the test as passed without analysis
Determine whether it is unreachable, unstimulated, or irrelevant before changing stimulus or waiving
questions.explanation: Coverage closure requires understanding the gap and preserving traceable justification for exclusions.

questions.question: How should reset behavior be represented in reusable agent documentation?
options: Ignore reset in passive mode
Tie reset into the factory name
Specify observed/drive sequencing, transaction flush behavior, and monitor restart assumptions
Assume reset is always synchronous and active high
questions.explanation: Users need clear reset semantics to compose agents and interpret scoreboard state correctly.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a reference model in a scoreboard?
options: Prevent all random traffic
Predict architecturally expected behavior from observed accepted inputs
Generate DUT clocks
Replace the monitor
questions.explanation: A model derives expected outputs/state independently so actual DUT observations can be checked.

questions.question: Which transaction is accepted by a ready/valid interface?
options: One sampled on an edge where VALID and READY are both asserted
Every item created by a sequence
An item with VALID high even when READY is low
Any payload that changes value
questions.explanation: Only the handshake establishes transfer; generated intent may never be accepted.

questions.question: Why should a regression impose timeouts?
options: Guarantee all tests pass
Avoid storing seeds
Make the DUT respond faster
Bound hangs and distinguish infrastructure deadlock from successful completion
questions.explanation: Bounded execution prevents a hung objection or missing response from consuming unbounded regression resources.

questions.question: A test passes only when run after another test. What likely issue deserves investigation?
options: The driver uses an analysis port
The simulator is deterministic
Hidden shared/global state or incomplete initialization causing order dependence
The test has too many bins
questions.explanation: Order-dependent results indicate non-isolated state, reset, resource, or configuration leakage between tests.

units.title: Cache and Memory Subsystem Design
units.description: Reason about cache geometry, coherence, miss handling, memory ordering, and measurable hierarchy performance.
units.content:
Cache architecture begins with explicit geometry and address decomposition. For capacity C bytes, line size B bytes, and S sets, associativity A satisfies C = S × A × B. A byte address splits into block offset, set index, and tag; when B and S are powers of two, their widths are log2(B) and log2(S). A line address is the byte address with offset removed. Confirm width arithmetic for parameterized configurations, especially when a width can be zero, and avoid truncating high address bits that distinguish physical aliases.

A lookup compares tags of valid ways in the indexed set. A hit returns data and updates replacement metadata; a miss allocates a miss-status entry, selects a victim, and may require writeback before refill. Dirty state indicates that memory is stale; evicting a dirty line requires preserving the complete line and address. Nonblocking caches support multiple outstanding misses, but then responses need IDs or ordered tracking, and requests to the same line may need merging. MSHR count, refill bandwidth, writeback buffering, and bank conflicts limit memory-level parallelism. A high hit rate alone does not guarantee high performance if miss latency, queueing, or bandwidth dominates.

Write policies interact: write-through sends each store downstream and often needs a write buffer; write-back marks a line dirty and defers traffic until eviction. Write-allocate fetches a line on a write miss; no-write-allocate may bypass allocation. Partial stores require byte enables and correct read-modify-write behavior when lower memory lacks byte writes. Uncached and strongly ordered regions must bypass or constrain speculative/cacheable paths as specified.

Coherence is necessary when multiple agents can cache shared writable data. A protocol establishes ownership and visibility, not merely a bus snoop signal. Ordering rules, fences, atomics, and device-memory semantics must be precise. Verification checks line-boundary accesses, aliases, eviction order, dirty writeback contents, simultaneous hits/misses, backpressure, reset, and coherence races. Performance analysis uses traces and queue occupancy to separate compulsory, capacity, conflict, and coherence misses. Data arrays, tags, ECC, replacement state, and refill/writeback paths all require independent integrity and timing consideration.
keyPoints: Derive tag/index/offset widths from capacity, associativity, line size, and address width.
Track valid, dirty, replacement, and outstanding-miss state with explicit invariants.
Specify write policy, byte-enable behavior, ordering, uncached regions, and coherence ownership.
Evaluate miss classes, MSHR/bank/bandwidth limits, and dirty writeback correctness.

test.objective: Demonstrate and verify cache and memory subsystem design behavior against the stated invariants.

questions.question: A cache has 32 KiB capacity, 64-byte lines, and 4 ways. How many sets?
questions.explanation: Sets = capacity/(line size×ways)=32768/(64×4)=128.

questions.question: For the same cache, how many offset bits are required?
questions.explanation: A 64-byte line requires log2(64)=6 low address bits for byte offset.

questions.question: For 48-bit byte addresses, 128 sets, 64-byte lines, what is tag width?
options: 35 bits
36 bits
41 bits
29 bits
questions.explanation: Tag bits = 48 - 7 index bits - 6 offset bits = 35.

questions.question: A dirty line is evicted in a write-back cache. What must the controller do?
options: Discard it because memory has the old value
Write only the tag bits
Invalidate all sets
Write the entire modified line to the correct lower-memory line address
questions.explanation: Dirty means lower memory may be stale, so preserve the line contents and address through writeback.

questions.question: What does a valid bit represent?
options: Whether the CPU request is aligned
Whether replacement state is least-recently-used
Whether the way currently contains an allocated meaningful cache line
Whether data has been modified
questions.explanation: Valid distinguishes initialized/allocated tag-data entries from invalid ways.

questions.question: A direct-mapped cache miss followed by access to an address with same index but different tag is likely what?
options: A byte-lane alias by definition
A conflict eviction
A compulsory hit
A coherence fence
questions.explanation: Distinct blocks mapping to one set conflict; in a direct-mapped cache the new tag replaces the prior line.

questions.question: What is the role of an MSHR?
options: Track an outstanding cache miss/refill and associated request state
Store the replacement policy only
Decode byte strobes
Replace dirty data with parity
questions.explanation: Miss-status holding registers allow outstanding misses and preserve their addresses/request context.

questions.question: Why can two misses to the same line be merged?
options: Tags become identical on every cache set
It eliminates the need for valid bits
It permits responses to be dropped
One refill can satisfy both requests if ordering and store merging are handled correctly
questions.explanation: Coalescing avoids redundant lower-level fetches, but dependent stores and response obligations still need tracking.

questions.question: Which combination describes write-through, no-write-allocate?
options: Mark dirty and never send stores
Allocate on reads only and discard all writes
Write every store downstream; a store miss bypasses line allocation
Write only on eviction; every miss allocates
questions.explanation: Write-through propagates each write; no-write-allocate does not install a missed line on store.

questions.question: Why does a partial store miss need careful treatment?
options: Dirty bits cannot represent partial bytes
Lower memory may not support byte enables, requiring correct merge/read-modify-write
Tag comparison stops working
The offset width becomes zero
questions.explanation: The subsystem must preserve untouched bytes if downstream write granularity is larger than the store.

questions.question: An access straddles a cache-line boundary. What should the interface/model do?
options: Split or explicitly support the access across both lines per contract
Silently wrap the byte offset
Use only the first line tag
Assume it cannot occur without checking alignment rules
questions.explanation: Cross-line accesses involve two line lookups/transactions unless prohibited by the architectural alignment contract.

questions.question: What is true of a cache hit rate as a performance metric?
options: It completely determines execution time
It is independent of workload locality
It proves coherence correctness
It does not capture miss penalty, queueing, bandwidth, or hit latency alone
questions.explanation: Average performance also depends on miss service time and throughput constraints.

questions.question: What does a fence primarily establish?
options: A replacement victim
A guarantee all stores are cache hits
Ordering constraints among specified memory operations
A cache-line size change
questions.explanation: Fences constrain architectural visibility/order; exact scope depends on the memory model and domain.

questions.question: What does coherence ownership represent?
options: The CPU’s instruction privilege level
Which agent may hold/write a line under the protocol’s visibility rules
Which way is least recently used
Which byte lane is selected
questions.explanation: Coherence states regulate sharing and exclusive modification, preserving a defined view among agents.

questions.question: Why are device/uncached regions treated differently from ordinary cacheable memory?
options: Side effects and ordering may forbid caching, speculation, or combining accesses
Device addresses never use physical address bits
They are always coherent automatically
They must use write-back policy
questions.explanation: Memory-mapped devices can have side effects, so their access and ordering semantics differ from normal memory.

questions.question: A cache has 4 MSHRs but one refill port. What likely constrains peak refill throughput?
options: The number of tag bits
The cache’s byte offset width
Dirty state prevents all hits
Refill-port service bandwidth may bottleneck despite multiple outstanding misses
questions.explanation: MSHRs expose concurrency, but a shared port can serialize actual data returns and limit throughput.

questions.question: Which test best detects missing dirty writeback address bits?
options: Reset with no requests
Change replacement policy without memory checking
Evict dirty lines at addresses differing only in high tag bits and compare lower-memory locations
Read the same line twice without eviction
questions.explanation: Incorrect address reconstruction can alias distinct lines during writeback; high-tag variation exposes truncation.

questions.question: What does an ECC/parity check on data arrays fail to cover by itself?
options: Any cache hit
Tag, valid/dirty metadata, replacement state, and protocol integrity
The payload bits
The data array only
questions.explanation: Data protection does not automatically protect metadata or control state, which can misroute corrupted data.

questions.question: A simultaneous read hit and refill target the same set. What must RTL define?
options: Array port conflicts and whether old data, new data, or arbitration wins
Only the CPU reset vector
AXI-Lite AW/W timing
The cache’s source clock frequency
questions.explanation: Bank/array collision semantics affect correctness and must be resolved by scheduling, bypass, or multiport structure.

questions.question: What distinguishes a compulsory miss from a capacity miss?
options: Compulsory is a dirty eviction; capacity is a coherence retry
They are identical categories
Capacity depends only on line offset width
Compulsory is first reference to a block; capacity arises when working set exceeds storage
questions.explanation: Compulsory misses occur on initial access; capacity misses result from insufficient total cache capacity for reuse.

units.title: Clock, Reset, and Power Intent
units.description: Integrate clock/reset architecture with isolation, retention, level shifting, and power-aware verification.
units.content:
Clock, reset, and power are architectural interfaces with sequencing contracts. Clock trees define frequency, phase, duty-cycle, uncertainty, and generated-clock relationships; RTL clock enables should generally preserve a recognized clock network rather than create arbitrary gated clocks. Integrated clock-gating cells latch enables in a safe phase to avoid glitches. A derived clock must be declared and constrained with its source relationship, and a clock mux must switch only under a characterized glitch-free protocol. Clock-domain analysis needs mode-specific active clocks, including test and low-power modes.

Reset strategy specifies assertion polarity, synchronicity, priority, per-domain release, reset values, and sequencing relative to power-good and clock-stable indications. A reset synchronizer solves release alignment in its receiving domain but cannot compensate for an unstable clock or a domain still power-gated. Reset values should put interfaces into a safe, non-accepting state. Reset deassertion and isolation removal are ordered events: do not expose unknown retained or unpowered state to active logic.

Power intent describes power domains, supply sets, legal power states, isolation boundaries, retention elements, and level shifters. Isolation clamps outputs from a shut-down source to a safe value before supply collapse, and remains asserted until source state is valid after restoration. Retention saves selected state before power-down and restores it before consumers use it; retained does not mean coherent with non-retained state. Level shifters are required where voltage domains demand them, with direction and power-state legality considered. UPF/CPF intent must match RTL hierarchy and implementation cell mapping; a syntactically accepted power file is not proof of a safe sequence.

Low-power entry and exit should be modeled as a protocol: quiesce traffic, drain or cancel outstanding work, save state, assert isolation, gate clocks if required, and remove power in an approved order. Wake-up reverses this with supply-good, clock stabilization, reset/restore, and isolation release. Verify interrupted transitions, asynchronous wake, brownout assumptions, and handshakes at boundaries. Power-aware simulation or formal checks should inject X behavior for off domains and verify clamps/retention, not simply force all signals to zero. Signoff correlates intent, power-aware simulation, structural checks, timing modes, and physical cell insertion.
keyPoints: Model legal clock modes, generated clocks, glitch-free switching, and test clocks explicitly.
Synchronize reset release per destination domain and sequence it after power/clock readiness.
Assert isolation before power collapse and release only after restored state is valid.
Verify power intent against RTL hierarchy, inserted cells, UPF states, and X-aware transition behavior.

test.objective: Demonstrate and verify clock, reset, and power intent behavior against the stated invariants.

questions.question: Why are ordinary combinational clock gates unsafe?
options: They increase clock period by definition
They remove setup timing
They synchronize asynchronous data
Enable changes can create glitches or shortened pulses on the clock
questions.explanation: A combinational enable transition while clock is active can generate an unintended edge; use characterized integrated gating.

questions.question: What must a generated clock constraint describe?
options: The reset polarity only
Its CDC waiver list
Its relationship/source and waveform or divide/multiply behavior
Only the name of the RTL module
questions.explanation: Timing analysis needs the generated clock’s source and phase/frequency relationship to analyze paths correctly.

questions.question: What does a reset synchronizer guarantee?
options: No reset recovery/removal checks are needed
Deassertion is aligned through stages to its destination clock, subject to a stable clock
The clock is stable before reset release
All domains leave reset simultaneously
questions.explanation: A local synchronizer coordinates release into one domain; it cannot guarantee another domain’s release or clock readiness.

questions.question: Why assert reset asynchronously in some designs but deassert synchronously?
options: Immediate assertion can force safety, while synchronized release avoids asynchronous recovery timing
Synchronous assertion is illegal
Asynchronous release avoids all metastability
Reset values are not sampled by flops
questions.explanation: Release near an active edge can violate recovery/removal; local synchronization mitigates that risk.

questions.question: When should isolation usually be asserted during power-down?
options: After the domain is fully powered off
Only when the destination clock is stopped
After isolation cells are removed
Before the source domain becomes invalid or loses supply
questions.explanation: Clamps must protect live logic from unknown/off-domain outputs before source behavior becomes unreliable.

questions.question: When may isolation safely be removed during power-up?
options: Before retention restoration
While reset is asserted to the destination only
After supply, clock, reset/restore, and source outputs are valid per sequence
Immediately when power-enable is requested
questions.explanation: Releasing the clamp too early can expose X or stale state; wait for valid restored source behavior.

questions.question: What is a retention flop intended to preserve?
options: State in every unpowered block automatically
Selected state across a power-domain shutdown/restore sequence
All combinational outputs without power
Clock phase across domains
questions.explanation: Retention applies to designated state elements and requires save/restore sequencing and supply support.

questions.question: Why might retained state still be inconsistent after wake-up?
options: Related non-retained state or external agents may have changed while the domain was off
Retention always corrupts every bit
Power intent cannot include state
Reset is synchronous
questions.explanation: Retained state may be stale relative to live domains and must be reconciled by architectural protocol.

questions.question: What is the function of a level shifter?
options: Synchronize asynchronous transitions
Isolate a shutoff domain to a clamp value
Retain register state
Translate signal voltage between domains within specified direction/range
questions.explanation: Voltage translation addresses electrical compatibility; it is distinct from isolation, which blocks invalid values.

questions.question: What is a robust low-power entry sequence?
options: Deassert reset, then stop clocks during active transactions
Release isolation before save
Quiesce/drain traffic, save state, assert isolation, then gate clocks/power as specified
Remove power first and inspect traffic afterward
questions.explanation: Quiescing and isolating prevent in-flight work and invalid outputs from escaping during collapse.

questions.question: What condition is essential before ungating a clock after wake?
options: No power-good indication is needed
Clock source is stable and mode selection is safe
All output signals are X
Isolation has already been removed regardless of reset
questions.explanation: Consumers must receive clean clock edges; the source and mux/gating state need characterized stability.

questions.question: How should power-aware verification model an off domain?
options: Allow unknown/off behavior and check isolation/retention boundaries
Force all off-domain outputs to zero without clamp checks
Keep the domain fully operational in simulation
Disable all assertions globally
questions.explanation: X injection exposes missing isolation and unsafe consumers instead of masking them with convenient zero values.

questions.question: If wake can arrive asynchronously, where should it be handled?
options: Only inside the powered-off clock domain
As a combinational clock input
By assuming it aligns with the clock
Through a safe always-on path with synchronized or handshake-controlled wake sequencing
questions.explanation: An off domain cannot reliably process a wake input; an always-on controller captures and sequences it.

questions.question: What is the purpose of UPF/CPF power-state tables?
options: Define cache replacement policy
Set simulation random seeds
Describe legal combinations/sequences of domain power states
Replace RTL functional specifications
questions.explanation: Power intent formalizes legal states and transitions for tools and implementation.

questions.question: What does a syntactically valid power intent file not prove?
options: That state tables exist
That hierarchy, supply mapping, sequencing, and inserted cells are correct
That the parser accepted its syntax
That power domains were named
questions.explanation: Consistency checks against actual RTL and implementation are still required.

questions.question: Why include test and scan clocks in clock-mode analysis?
options: They create operating modes and paths with different clock relationships
Scan has no timing impact
They change only data polarity
It eliminates generated clocks
questions.explanation: Mode-specific clocks affect constraints, CDC structure, and timing closure during test operation.

questions.question: What is the danger of deasserting reset before power-good?
options: It shortens setup time safely
It guarantees retained data integrity
It makes isolation unnecessary
Flops may not have valid supply and can enter unpredictable state
questions.explanation: Reset behavior assumes powered circuitry; reset release must follow supply readiness.

questions.question: Which ordering best protects restored state from consumers?
options: Ungate all clocks before power-good
Clear retention before restoring data
Restore and validate source state while isolation remains asserted, then release clamp
Release isolation before supply stabilization
questions.explanation: Holding isolation during restore prevents consumers observing intermediate or invalid values.

questions.question: Why must power intent and physical implementation be correlated?
options: It eliminates IR-drop analysis
The flow must insert correct isolation, retention, and level-shifter cells at mapped boundaries
UPF changes RTL syntax
It determines software cacheability automatically
questions.explanation: Intent only describes requirements; implementation must map them to real cells and verify placement/connectivity.

questions.question: What failure is likely if a clock mux switches asynchronously between two active clocks?
options: A runt or extra clock pulse can corrupt sequential state
The clocks become phase-locked
All flops automatically reset
Only combinational paths are affected
questions.explanation: An uncontrolled transition can produce malformed edges; use glitch-free switching with safe source handoff.

units.title: Timing Closure and Physical Implementation
units.description: Close timing by connecting constraints, static analysis, placement/routing effects, and disciplined optimization.
units.content:
Static timing analysis (STA) checks path delays against clock constraints without enumerating input vectors. A setup check compares the latest data arrival with the capture edge minus setup time and uncertainty; a hold check compares earliest data arrival with the same-edge capture requirement plus hold time. Launch and capture clock latency/skew affect both checks, often in opposite directions. Positive setup slack does not imply hold safety.
