Constraints must define clocks, generated clocks, input/output delays, uncertainty, false and multicycle paths, and operating corners; missing or overbroad exceptions make reports misleading.

A multicycle path is a functional timing exception only when the design guarantees the destination is not required to sample on intervening edges. Setup multicycle changes often require a corresponding hold adjustment to preserve intended edge separation. A false path is appropriate only when no functional timing relationship exists, such as a properly synchronized asynchronous input before its first stage; it must not hide ordinary synchronous paths. Review unconstrained endpoints, exception coverage, and clock interaction reports before interpreting a green summary.

Physical delay includes cell delay, interconnect, slew, load, and coupling. Placement and routing change wire delay and capacitance; high fanout control nets may need buffering or replication. Congestion causes detours, degraded slew, and longer paths. Clock-tree synthesis inserts clock buffers and skew that alter path budgets. Setup repair may upsize cells or restructure logic, increasing area, power, and hold risk. Hold repair inserts delay, potentially consuming setup margin. Optimization is iterative and corner-dependent; repair at one corner may worsen another.

The critical path must be classified: logic depth, high fanout, poor placement, memory access, clock uncertainty, or an invalid constraint. Optimize the true dominant component rather than blindly adding pipeline stages or upsizing. Pipelining changes latency and requires protocol/verification updates; retiming can affect reset and equivalence assumptions. Timing closure includes setup/hold across modes and corners, signal integrity, clock checks, transition/capacitance/fanout limits, and physical verification. Preserve reports and constraint revisions so signoff demonstrates the delivered netlist, not an earlier RTL snapshot.
keyPoints: Audit clocks, I/O delays, exceptions, corners, and unconstrained endpoints before timing optimization.
Analyze setup and hold independently; skew and repair affect them differently.
Use multicycle/false-path exceptions only when architectural behavior proves them valid.
Correlate timing changes with routed parasitics, congestion, power, equivalence, and delivered netlist.

test.objective: Demonstrate and verify timing closure and physical implementation behavior against the stated invariants.

questions.question: What does positive setup slack establish for a path?
options: The setup requirement is met under the analyzed constraints/corner
The hold requirement is met too
The path is functionally correct
All operating corners meet timing
questions.explanation: Setup and hold are separate checks; passing one does not imply passing the other or other corners.

questions.question: What is a setup timing check fundamentally comparing?
options: Earliest arrival against same-edge hold requirement
Only clock period against cell area
Input voltage against output slew
Latest data arrival against required capture time
questions.explanation: Setup uses maximum data delay and required capture timing including setup time, uncertainty, and clock effects.

questions.question: What physical effect can worsen hold after clock-tree synthesis?
options: Increasing logical vector width without routing
Changing only the output filename
Capture/launch skew and minimum data-path delay relationship
A longer setup uncertainty alone
questions.explanation: Clock insertion delays change relative edge arrival; hold depends on earliest data and skew.

questions.question: When is a false path exception defensible?
options: To ignore a high-fanout synchronous control path
No functional timing relationship exists for that path, with a justified architectural reason
Whenever STA reports negative slack
Whenever two signals have different names
questions.explanation: Exceptions must represent actual design intent; using them to hide a violation invalidates analysis.

questions.question: Why can a multicycle setup exception need a matching hold adjustment?
options: Changing setup edge separation can otherwise impose unintended hold relationship
Hold checks are disabled by any setup exception
It changes clock frequency
It prevents CDC analysis
questions.explanation: The setup multicycle changes the capture edge; corresponding hold semantics must reflect the intended launch/capture relationship.

questions.question: A timing summary is green but many endpoints are unconstrained. What conclusion is valid?
options: All paths meet timing by default
Unconstrained paths are automatically false
Only hold checks need rerun
Signoff is incomplete until those endpoints are constrained or justified
questions.explanation: STA cannot establish required timing on endpoints without appropriate constraints.

questions.question: What is the effect of interconnect parasitics on timing?
options: They eliminate clock uncertainty
They affect only hold, never setup
Wire resistance/capacitance add delay and can degrade slew
They change RTL boolean function
questions.explanation: Routed wire delay and loading contribute to both max/min path timing and transition quality.

questions.question: Why can high fanout cause a critical path?
options: It removes setup constraints
Driver load and routing/buffering add delay and congestion
It makes all destinations share one register
It reduces clock period automatically
questions.explanation: Large fanout burdens drivers and physical routing; buffering/replication can help with area/power tradeoffs.

questions.question: What is a common setup-repair side effect of aggressive cell upsizing?
options: More power/area and potentially worsened hold or congestion
Guaranteed hold improvement
Reduced input toggle rate
No physical impact after synthesis
questions.explanation: Stronger cells can raise power and loading and may affect placement, other paths, and min-delay closure.

questions.question: What does hold repair typically add?
options: A new functional pipeline stage by default
Clock period reduction
A false-path exception
Minimum delay such as buffers on too-fast paths
questions.explanation: Delay cells/buffers increase minimum path delay to satisfy hold, possibly consuming setup margin.

questions.question: A path is critical due primarily to routing detour in a congested region. What is the first category of fix to evaluate?
options: Add an unrelated pipeline register
Set a multicycle exception
Placement/congestion and locality, not only Boolean depth
Change the reset polarity
questions.explanation: The dominant delay is physical interconnect; locality and congestion changes target the actual bottleneck.

questions.question: What can pipelining a critical combinational path change?
options: The source clock frequency automatically
Architectural latency and protocol/verification behavior
Only gate count, never observable behavior
Clock uncertainty only
questions.explanation: A pipeline register adds cycles and may require interface, ordering, and testbench updates.

questions.question: Why must timing be checked across multiple corners?
options: Process, voltage, temperature, and variation alter cell and interconnect delays
Only one corner has a clock
All corners have identical setup time
STA randomly chooses corners
questions.explanation: Different PVT corners can be worst for max delay, min delay, and power; closure is multi-corner.

questions.question: What does clock uncertainty model?
options: Exact data path delay
The number of reset synchronizer stages
Logic equivalence
Margin for jitter, variation, and other clock-timing uncertainty per methodology
questions.explanation: Uncertainty reduces available timing budget to account for nonideal clock behavior and variation.

questions.question: Why inspect clock interaction reports?
options: They report only fanout
They determine cache hit rate
They show relationships/analysis status between clock domains and may reveal missing or invalid assumptions
They replace all path reports
questions.explanation: Clock interaction analysis surfaces asynchronous, exclusive, or unconstrained clock relationships that need explicit handling.

questions.question: Why can a high-fanout net replication improve timing but harm power?
options: It lowers clock frequency
Duplicating drivers reduces load/distance but adds cells and switching capacitance
Replication removes the signal
It eliminates all glitches by definition
questions.explanation: Physical replication trades local drive and wire length against additional area and dynamic/leakage power.

questions.question: What should be rerun after a timing-driven RTL or constraint change?
options: Relevant STA and equivalence/functional verification for the delivered configuration
Only code formatting
No signoff because intent is unchanged
Only simulation waveform viewing
questions.explanation: Design or exception changes can affect behavior and timing; regenerate correlated evidence on the final netlist.

questions.question: What is the danger of broad false-pathing an entire clock domain?
options: It makes the design slower
It changes asynchronous input voltage
It creates additional hold buffers automatically
Legitimate synchronous or constrained crossings can disappear from analysis
questions.explanation: A broad exception can hide paths that should be timed or structurally analyzed.

questions.question: Which delay matters for setup closure?
options: Average delay across all paths
Clock-to-Q at one unrelated endpoint
Maximum data path delay at the applicable setup corner
Minimum data delay only
questions.explanation: Setup is a max-delay requirement; min-delay analysis addresses hold separately.

questions.question: A path meets timing in synthesis but fails after route. Why is this plausible?
options: A routed path has no capacitance
Routed wire parasitics, congestion, and clock-tree effects are absent or estimated earlier
Routing changes Boolean logic necessarily
Synthesis does not use clocks
questions.explanation: Post-route implementation introduces actual interconnect and clock effects that alter delay.

units.title: Parameterized Reusable IP and Contracts
units.description: Create reusable configurable RTL with mathematically safe parameterization, explicit interfaces, and verifiable integration contracts.
units.content:
Reusable IP is defined by a contract, not by parameter count. Document legal parameter ranges, reset behavior, clocking, protocol rules, latency, throughput, error handling, and unsupported combinations. Parameters that alter widths, depths, or generate topology need elaboration-time checks and boundary tests. `$clog2(1)` is zero, so expressions such as `[ADDR_W-1:0]` or `[ $clog2(DEPTH)-1:0 ]` can become illegal or silently create surprising widths. Use explicit minimum widths and handle depth-one cases deliberately. Avoid unsized literals and implicit signedness in address arithmetic; size constants to operands and define overflow behavior.

A parameterized FIFO, for example, must define whether DEPTH must be a power of two, pointer width, full detection, simultaneous push/pop semantics, and behavior at DEPTH=1. A memory array indexed by a pointer is not enough: prove pointers remain in range and that occupancy is between zero and DEPTH. `DEPTH` and `WIDTH` should be checked positive, while unsupported combinations should fail elaboration clearly rather than produce obscure downstream errors. Width conversions between external interfaces and internal arithmetic should be explicit and lint-clean.

Interfaces and modports can encode directional intent, but tool portability and synthesis support must be considered. A transaction-level interface should describe handshake and payload stability; a module’s contract should state which side drives ready/valid and whether combinational paths are allowed. Reset is part of the contract: async assertion/sync release, reset values, and in-flight transaction handling must be known. Error outputs need defined behavior, not X as a placeholder. Parameter defaults should support common use without becoming undocumented assumptions.

Verification uses a configuration matrix: minimum and maximum supported widths/depths, non-power-of-two values if allowed, feature toggles, and corner combinations. Elaboration tests catch illegal dimensions; simulation/formal tests check semantic invariants. Lint and synthesis validate multiple configurations, because generate branches may otherwise remain uncompiled. Equivalence should compare the intended configurations, not just defaults. Versioning records interface compatibility and parameter changes; integrations should pin a known IP revision and machine-readable configuration. Reuse becomes reliable when assumptions and guarantees travel with the block and are executable in assertions and tests.
units.example:
module param_fifo #(parameter int W=8, DEPTH=4, localparam int PW=(DEPTH<=1)?1:$clog2(DEPTH))
(input logic clk,rst_n,input logic push,pop,input logic [W-1:0] din,output logic [W-1:0] dout,output logic full,empty);
 initial begin if(W<1 || DEPTH<1) $fatal(1,"W and DEPTH must be positive"); end
 logic [W-1:0] mem[DEPTH]; int unsigned count; int unsigned wr,rd;
 assign empty=(count==0); assign full=(count==DEPTH); assign dout=mem[rd];
 always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
  if(!rst_n) begin count<=0; wr<=0; rd<=0; end
  else begin
   if(push&&!full) begin mem[wr]<=din; wr<=(wr==DEPTH-1)?0:wr+1; end
   if(pop&&!empty) rd<=(rd==DEPTH-1)?0:rd+1;
   case ({push&&!full,pop&&!empty}) 2'b10:count<=count+1; 2'b01:count<=count-1; default:count<=count; endcase
  end
 end
endmodule
keyPoints: Document a legal parameter domain and reject unsupported values at elaboration.
Guard zero-width `$clog2` and explicitly handle depth-one/non-power-of-two configurations.
Make signedness, sizing, overflow, reset, handshake, latency, and error behavior part of the IP contract.
Validate configuration corners through elaboration, lint, simulation/formal, synthesis, and revision-controlled integration.

test.objective: Demonstrate and verify parameterized reusable ip and contracts behavior against the stated invariants.

questions.question: What is the result of `$clog2(1)` in SystemVerilog?
options: Undefined in every tool
questions.explanation: The mathematical ceiling of log2(1) is zero; directly using it as a vector width can create an invalid or tool-dependent range.

questions.question: How should a pointer width be defined for a depth-one FIFO?
options: Use an explicit minimum width of one and special-case wrap/full logic
Use a zero-bit pointer
Use `$clog2(DEPTH)+2` without review
Make the data width equal to DEPTH
questions.explanation: A zero-width pointer is not a useful portable vector; depth one requires explicit handling.

questions.question: Which statement must be part of a reusable FIFO contract?
options: The author’s preferred editor
Only the default data value
The synthesis tool’s theme
Whether DEPTH must be power of two and how simultaneous push/pop behaves
questions.explanation: Parameter legality and corner behavior affect architecture and integration, so they must be explicit.

questions.question: Why can unsized literals be dangerous in parameterized arithmetic?
options: They force clock gating
They automatically prevent overflow
Their default sizing/signedness can cause unintended extension or truncation
They are always 1-bit unsigned
questions.explanation: Implicit integer sizing can alter comparisons and arithmetic; explicit widths/signs make intent portable.

questions.question: What assertion captures FIFO occupancy range?
options: pop |-> full
0 <= count && count <= DEPTH
count == DEPTH always
push |-> count unchanged
questions.explanation: Bounded occupancy is a fundamental invariant independent of traffic sequence.

questions.question: Why test a non-power-of-two FIFO depth?
options: Pointer wrap and address range logic may fail when natural binary overflow does not equal DEPTH
It changes payload endian order
It disables asynchronous reset
It guarantees empty is never true
questions.explanation: For depth three, a two-bit pointer naturally reaches index three, which is invalid unless explicitly wrapped.

questions.question: How should unsupported parameter values fail?
options: Silently truncate dimensions
Drive all outputs X forever
Wait for a runtime request to fail
With a clear elaboration or initialization-time diagnostic
questions.explanation: Early explicit validation is easier to diagnose and avoids ambiguous generated hardware.

questions.question: Which configuration matrix is most useful?
options: Every possible integer to 32-bit maximum
One random configuration with no record
Boundary/legal combinations, feature toggles, and width/depth extremes
Only the default parameters
questions.explanation: Targeted boundary and interaction cases exercise generate branches and arithmetic risks efficiently.

questions.question: What is a risk in `logic [W-1:0]` if W is zero?
options: It disables the module clock
An invalid or unexpectedly ranged packed array declaration
It automatically means an empty bus portably
It creates a valid parity bit
questions.explanation: Zero-width vectors are not a safe portable interface; enforce W>=1 or define a deliberate alternative.

questions.question: Why should address arithmetic declare signedness?
options: To avoid sign extension or comparison errors for high-bit addresses
Signed values never overflow
Unsigned addresses cannot be parameterized
It improves CDC MTBF
questions.explanation: Mixed signed and unsigned expressions can produce incorrect range checks or truncation at parameterized widths.

questions.question: What should a module contract say about reset and in-flight items?
options: Only the reset pin name
That reset is irrelevant to protocol
That all parameterizations use the same reset value without checking
Reset polarity/timing and whether outstanding transactions are flushed or preserved
questions.explanation: Integrators and scoreboards need to know how reset affects visible transactions and state.

questions.question: Why compile multiple parameter values in lint/synthesis?
options: Lint checks only comments
It guarantees functional correctness automatically
Generate branches and width-dependent constructs may be untested at defaults
Synthesis changes parameter values at runtime
questions.explanation: Elaboration is configuration-specific; alternate branches may contain errors or infer unintended hardware.

questions.question: A parameter controls an address width. What is a critical range check?
options: Ensure width is less than one
Ensure width covers every legal address without overflow/truncation
Ensure width is always equal to data width
Ensure width is even
questions.explanation: Address capacity depends on legal range; too-narrow arithmetic aliases or truncates addresses.

questions.question: What does an interface modport provide?
options: Directional views of interface signals for different participants
Automatic protocol correctness
A clock-domain synchronizer
A memory implementation
questions.explanation: Modports encode which interface signals a role may drive or observe.

questions.question: Why might a reusable block avoid unsupported interface syntax?
options: Interfaces cannot express any signals
It prevents all parameterization
It improves cache hit rate
Synthesis/simulator portability varies across toolchains
questions.explanation: Language-feature support differences can block integrations; supported subset should be verified in target tools.

questions.question: What is an appropriate FIFO full behavior on simultaneous accepted pop and push?
options: Always overflow count to DEPTH+1
Clear all entries
Permit replacement if the contract allows capacity freed on that edge
Always reject push because old count is full
questions.explanation: With a valid simultaneous dequeue, storage is freed at the edge; logic can accept replacement if correctly implemented.

questions.question: Why pin an IP revision and configuration in SoC integration?
options: Because parameters cannot change between builds
To make the exact interface/parameter contract reproducible
To avoid running simulation
To prevent any future updates
questions.explanation: Version and config capture identify the validated implementation used by integration.

questions.question: Which is stronger evidence than checking only default simulation?
options: Elaboration plus functional checks over supported parameter boundaries and feature combinations
A successful file open
A single passing test with W=8
A green code formatter
questions.explanation: Boundary/configuration tests expose elaboration and behavioral failures that defaults miss.

questions.question: What should happen to unstrobed byte lanes in a parameterized register bank?
options: Always clear to zero
Copy from the next word
Become signed
Remain unchanged unless the contract specifies another behavior
questions.explanation: Byte-enable semantics must be explicit and preserved regardless of configured data width.

questions.question: Why include unsupported combinations in parameter documentation?
options: To replace assertion coverage
To make the default unknown
Integrators can reject them early rather than relying on accidental tool behavior
To encourage invalid configurations
questions.explanation: Explicit exclusions are part of a reliable reusable contract and prevent accidental dependence on undefined configurations.

units.title: SoC Integration, Debug, and Signoff
units.description: Integrate heterogeneous IP with traceable contracts, system-level observability, failure triage, and release evidence.
units.content:
SoC integration is the discipline of preserving component contracts across hierarchy. Address maps need aligned regions, non-overlapping decode, access permissions, security attribution, and documented behavior for unmapped addresses. Interconnect topology determines arbitration, ordering, outstanding capacity, and response routing. Clock/reset and power-domain boundaries must agree with the blocks’ assumptions; a module verified in isolation can fail when reset sequencing, bus pressure, or address aliases differ at top level. Pin down interface widths, endian conventions, ID handling, burst support, error responses, and performance limits in machine-checkable integration data.

Integration verification should include connectivity and structural checks, protocol assertions, address-map tests, security and privilege tests, and end-to-end software-visible scenarios. A transaction scoreboard spanning initiator to target detects routing, alias, and response-ID errors that block-level tests miss. Stress independent channel stalls, simultaneous masters, backpressure, reset during traffic, low-power transitions, and error propagation. Constrained random tests should be complemented by directed tests for rare but high-consequence cases. Assertions and covergroups should map to system requirements, with every waiver and unreachable condition owned and reviewed.

Debug depends on observability designed in advance. Useful evidence includes transaction IDs, timestamps/cycle counts, bus performance counters, reset cause, timeout/error status, trace buffers, and synchronized event logs. Instrumentation must avoid perturbing timing or leaking protected data. A failure is localized by finding the first divergence across layers: software intent, bus request, interconnect route, target acceptance, internal state transition, and response. Preserve seeds, build hashes, parameter configurations, firmware, constraints, and waveforms. Avoid masking a failure by adding retries or weakening checks before the root cause is understood.

Signoff is a cross-domain evidence package: RTL and gate-level functional verification, CDC/RDC, formal proofs, lint, synthesis/STA across modes and corners, DFT, low-power checks, security review, physical verification, and software compatibility. Results must correspond to the exact source revision, constraints, UPF, libraries, and implementation database. Change impact analysis determines which evidence must be refreshed after a modification. Release gates should list open waivers, known limitations, performance margins, safety mechanisms, and rollback plan. “All tests passed” is not signoff unless the tested configuration is the shipped one and requirements have traceable closure.
units.example:
module decode2 #(parameter int AW=16)(input logic [AW-1:0] addr,input logic req,output logic hit_a,hit_b,miss);
 always_comb begin
  hit_a=req && (addr[AW-1:12]==0);       // 0x0000-0x0fff
  hit_b=req && (addr[AW-1:12]==1);       // 0x1000-0x1fff
  miss=req && !(hit_a||hit_b);
 end
endmodule
keyPoints: Specify address, security, ordering, clock/reset/power, throughput, and error-response contracts end to end.
Verify the integrated route from initiator acceptance through target response, including aliases and contention.
Build debug observability and reproducible artifacts into the integration plan.
Tie signoff evidence and waivers to the exact delivered RTL, constraints, libraries, power intent, and implementation.

test.objective: Demonstrate and verify soc integration, debug, and signoff behavior against the stated invariants.

questions.question: Why are address-map boundaries a high-value SoC test target?
options: They guarantee a CDC violation
They validate only software compilation
Decode off-by-one errors can alias adjacent targets or produce incorrect unmapped responses
They change AXI ready semantics
questions.explanation: Testing start/end boundaries and neighboring unmapped addresses exposes range and alignment mistakes.

questions.question: What is a transaction ID primarily used for in an interconnect?
options: Replace access permissions
Route and associate responses with outstanding requests under the protocol rules
Select clock frequency
Encode byte order automatically
questions.explanation: IDs preserve request/response association, especially when multiple transactions are outstanding.

questions.question: What is a system-level test that block tests often miss?
options: Two initiators contending for one target with independent stalls and response routing
A register reset test in isolation only
A combinational adder truth table
A single cache hit with no bus traffic
questions.explanation: Integration contention exercises arbitration, buffering, fairness, and cross-block response routing.

questions.question: What security property should an address decode enforce?
options: All addresses are publicly accessible
Decode depends only on low byte bits
Responses always return OKAY
Target access follows privilege/security attribution and mapped permissions
questions.explanation: Correct mapping alone is insufficient if unauthorized initiators can reach protected targets.

questions.question: Why define unmapped-address behavior explicitly?
options: It chooses endianness
It prevents setup violations
Masters need deterministic error/timeout semantics and software-visible diagnostics
Unmapped requests cannot occur
questions.explanation: Undefined handling can hang systems or mask decode defects; a contract should specify response and side effects.

questions.question: What is the best first debug strategy for an end-to-end mismatch?
options: Increase retry count until it passes
Find the earliest layer where observed behavior diverges from expected intent
Change every block simultaneously
Disable scoreboards
questions.explanation: The first divergence narrows causal ownership and avoids masking downstream symptoms.

questions.question: Which artifacts enable reproducible SoC failure triage?
options: Seed, source/build hash, parameters, firmware, constraints, and trace/waveform
Only a screenshot
The test name alone
A list of passed tests
questions.explanation: Failures depend on build/configuration and randomized state; preserve enough context to reproduce the exact run.

questions.question: Why can a retry conceal a root cause?
options: Retries always improve determinism
It proves address decode correct
It eliminates response ordering
It may hide a lost/duplicated transaction or timeout without fixing the failure mechanism
questions.explanation: Retry logic can make symptoms intermittent while leaving correctness or safety defects unresolved.

questions.question: What does an end-to-end scoreboard add beyond a local protocol checker?
options: Replaces all reset checks
Guarantees timing closure
Checks routing and functional response correspondence across initiator-to-target path
Checks only signal widths
questions.explanation: Local protocol compliance does not ensure requests reached the intended target or received correct results.

questions.question: What is change-impact analysis for signoff?
options: Assume all prior signoff remains valid
Identify which evidence must be rerun based on modified logic, constraints, or implementation
Delete stale reports without rerunning
Re-run only the fastest simulation
questions.explanation: A change can invalidate different analyses depending on its effect; explicit impact assessment keeps evidence current.

questions.question: Which item must match the released configuration for signoff?
options: Source revision, constraints, UPF, libraries, and implementation database
Only the project name
A developer’s local waveform color
The default parameter set regardless of shipped values
questions.explanation: Timing and implementation proofs apply to the exact design and environment that were analyzed.

questions.question: What observability signal is especially useful for tracing a bus timeout?
options: Only an uncorrelated activity LED
A random status bit
An unrelated clock enable
Request/response IDs and cycle timestamps or counters
questions.explanation: IDs and timing correlate the missing request/response across boundaries and quantify timeout behavior.

questions.question: What risk does debug instrumentation pose?
options: It guarantees formal convergence
It removes reset sequencing
It can perturb timing, area, power, or expose sensitive data
It always fixes bus deadlocks
questions.explanation: Instrumentation must be designed and reviewed so it does not invalidate implementation or security requirements.

questions.question: Why test reset asserted during active traffic?
options: It guarantees all targets idle
It exercises abort/flush semantics and prevents stale responses after restart
It validates only the reset pin polarity
The bus protocol is suspended forever
questions.explanation: System reset can intersect outstanding transactions, so the contract must define cleanup and recovery behavior.

questions.question: What should coverage closure demonstrate?
options: Specified scenarios were exercised and checked or justified with approved exclusions
Every possible input vector was simulated
All cover bins were forced reachable
No assertions ever fired
questions.explanation: Coverage must map to requirements and verified outcomes; exclusions need reasoned ownership.

questions.question: How should a security failure in a trace be triaged?
options: Assume the target is always responsible
Disable privilege checking for replay
Treat the error as a normal timeout
Check initiator attribution, interconnect policy, target checks, and response behavior
questions.explanation: Access control may be enforced at multiple boundaries; trace the attribute and authorization decision end to end.

questions.question: Why include performance counters in an SoC?
options: They automatically tune clock speed
They prove deadlock absence
They help separate arbitration, queueing, target latency, and bandwidth bottlenecks
They replace functional checks
questions.explanation: Measured occupancy and latency at boundaries localize performance constraints rather than relying on aggregate throughput.

questions.question: What does a signoff waiver need?
options: A promise that the issue will not recur
Precise scope, evidence/rationale, owner, and review/expiry policy
A broad wildcard and no owner
A matching test name only
questions.explanation: Traceable waivers prevent unjustified exceptions from silently hiding future defects.

questions.question: Why does RTL passing simulation not establish physical signoff?
options: It does not prove routed timing, DFT, power intent, physical rules, or final-netlist behavior
